name: Verne Island
lines: The Mysterious Island
the balloon's torn car, on the beach by the Chimneys (Lincoln Island)
We shall want everything. Let us begin at the beginning.
I am writing it all down. Someone will want to read it.
Ahoy! What does the captain want of us today?
Look! Do you know what that bird is? I do!
My master will know what to do.
The beach where the balloon came down
The foot of Granite House
The Mercy, by its mouth
The shore of Lake Grant
The slope of Mount Franklin
The crater of Mount Franklin
The clay of the Mercy's bank
The windmill on the plateau
The forests of the Far West
The Serpentine Peninsula
The sea cave in the black rocks
The telegraph line
Jules Verne · The Mysterious Island 🏝️ The end of the book
There, to conclude, all were happy, united in the present as they had been in the past; but never could they forget that island upon which they had arrived poor and friendless
The Bonadventure brings you home to the mouth of the Mercy.
🏝️ Tabor Island. A low islet, six miles round, a hill in the middle, a fringe of sand, and woods; and, at the back of a little hill, a hut of planks.
Captain Grant's hut
🛖 A table, a bed, a hearth, a few tools gone to rust; dust on everything.
It is a long time since this room has been inhabited," observed Herbert.
sail home to Lincoln Island
Falling into the Pacific
A ballast sack, empty
The 23rd of March, 1865, four in the evening, over the Pacific
🎈 Out of the clouds
Are we rising again?" "No. On the contrary." "Are we descending?" "Worse than that, captain! we are falling!
Such were the loud and startling words which resounded through the air, above the vast watery desert of the Pacific, about four o'clock in the evening of the 23rd of March, 1865.
▶ Heave out the ballast!
The balloon is losing gas and falling to the sea. What do the five throw out of the car, to keep it in the air?
Everything: the ballast, the provisions, the arms, and at last two thousand dollars in gold
Nothing: they wait for the wind
They would have been in the sea.
Is everything thrown out?" "No, here are still 2,000 dollars in gold.
It goes over the side.
The ballast went over the side as the balloon dragged along the sea. Some of it has rolled up the beach with the waves. Pick up five stones: they show where the car came down.
A grey stone from the balloon's last sack.
Stand on the beach where the car struck, and look at the sea where the waves took one of them away.
🌊 Four on the shore
But the car had contained five passengers, with a dog, and the balloon only left four on the shore.
The engineer, Cyrus Harding, was carried off by a wave as the net gave way; his dog Top leapt out after him.
The balloon had flown for five days, from Richmond in Virginia. Where have they come down?
Somewhere in the Pacific, seven thousand miles from home, on land no one of them knows
On the coast of Virginia
A pocket-watch in the sand
Someone's pocket-watch, dropped as they scrambled out of the car. Pick it up: it will matter, later.
The four call along the shore in the dusk: the engineer's name, and his dog's. Only the sea answers.
▶ The prisoners of Richmond
The Prisoners of Richmond
A page of the New York Herald
Richmond, Virginia, five days before: the siege
They were prisoners of war whose boldness had induced them to escape in this extraordinary manner.
Richmond was the Southern capital, besieged by General Grant's army; they were Northerners, held inside it.
The reporter is sitting on a rock, writing by the last light. Ask him who he is.
For ten years Gideon Spilett had been the reporter of the New York Herald, which he enriched by his letters and drawings, for he was as skilful in the use of the pencil as of the pen.
He was taken while sketching the battle, and Cyrus Harding was taken with him.
The sailor is staring out to sea, his jaw set. Ask him how the escape began.
He tells you how he went up to the engineer in the street, a stranger, and asked him straight out:
Captain Harding, will you try to escape?
By that lazy balloon which is left there doing nothing, and which looks to me as if it was waiting on purpose for us—
The boy is shivering in his wet jacket. Ask him how he came to be in the balloon.
Herbert is fifteen, the son of Pencroft's old captain, an orphan; Pencroft looks after him as if he were his own. He was in Richmond with the sailor, and where Pencroft goes, he goes.
Neb will not sit down. He keeps walking to the edge of the water. Speak to him.
Neb was born in Harding's household; the engineer freed him long ago, and he has never left his side. He got into Richmond on purpose, to be a prisoner with his master.
Harding had told Pencroft: Neb comes too.
▶ 'We will find him'
🌪️ The night of the 20th
How did they get into the balloon, under the guards' noses?
In the dark and the storm, at half-past nine at night, when nobody believed a balloon could go up in such a wind
They bribed the guards
At half-past nine, Harding and his companions glided from different directions into the square, which the gas-lamps, extinguished by the wind, had left in total obscurity.
A page of the Herald, blown ashore
A page from Spilett's notebook, soaked: a sketch of Richmond in the siege. Save it for him.
They have nothing: no food, no fire, no shelter, and the engineer is gone. And one of them cannot sit still.
▶ Search for the engineer
A shell from the islet
The 24th of March: the first night ashore
Ask Pencroft whether the engineer could have swum ashore.
Can he swim?" asked Pencroft.
Yes," replied Neb, "and besides, Top is there.
Then there's hope, says the sailor.
▶ Search the shore
Walk north along the beach, calling for him, as far as the rocks.
The sailor was right; they had been thrown, not on a continent, not even on an island, but on an islet which was not more than two miles in length, with even a less breadth.
A channel of sea lies between them and the bigger land across the water.
▶ Cross at low tide
How can they get across the channel to the mainland?
Wait for the ebb tide, when the channel is shallow enough to wade
Swim it in the dark
Build a boat out of nothing
Neb does, but he is not thinking.
But now the ebb is evidently making. In three hours we will attempt the passage
Neb did not wait for the ebb: he swam across. Find him on the far side.
Neb will not come back to rest. He will search the coast to the north all night, alone.
A shell from the rocks
Pick up five shells from the rocks at the water's edge: it's all there is to eat.
A long narrow shell, shut tight.
Towards midnight the stars come out. What do they tell Spilett?
That these are not the stars of the Northern Hemisphere: they are far south of the Equator
Nothing: the stars are the same everywhere
That it is going to rain
Towards midnight the stars shone out, and if the engineer had been there with his companions he would have remarked that these stars did not belong to the Northern Hemisphere.
Wait on the shore with the others for the dawn.
There is no sign of Cyrus Harding anywhere. They must find shelter, food and fire, and keep looking.
A rock-pigeon's egg
The 25th of March: the granite cliff
Pencroft has found mussels on the rocks. Go and see.
Here are mussels!" cried the sailor; "these will do instead of eggs!
They are not mussels," replied Herbert, who was attentively examining the molluscs attached to the rocks; "they are lithodomes.
What are lithodomes, that Herbert knows from his books?
Shellfish that bore holes into rock to live in, good to eat
Walk south along the foot of the cliff to where a river runs out to sea.
Drag six pieces of dead wood out of the river's edge: you will need a raft to carry them, and fuel for a fire.
Dead wood, washed down the river.
Back at the cliff, a heap of fallen granite blocks makes passages and holes like a chimney-stack. Go in.
Fallen blocks of granite, piled against the cliff, with winding passages between them where the wind roars. Pencroft stops up the worst holes with sand and stones: it is the best shelter they have.
Herbert has seen birds nesting in the holes of the cliff. Find four eggs among the rocks.
A rock-pigeon's egg, still warm.
Stop up the draughts in the Chimneys with sand and stones.
Eggs, shellfish, a shelter. But no fire, and no engineer: and Spilett has gone after Neb, to the north.
The 25th of March, evening
Pencroft is going through his pockets for the third time. Ask him what is wrong.
No matches. The box went over with everything else.
Certainly," replied Pencroft, "and I may say happily, for without matches or tinder we should be in a fix.
▶ Search the pockets again
Herbert says: look again, everywhere. Where might a match be?
In the lining of a waistcoat pocket, where small things slip
Dry moss and twigs
One match. Everything must be ready before it is struck. Gather five handfuls of dry moss and twigs from the cliff's foot.
Pencroft must not waste the match in the draught of the Chimneys. What does he do?
Twists a scrap of paper into a cone to shelter the flame, as smokers do in a high wind, and pushes it into the moss
Strikes it outside in the wind
Gives it to Herbert to hold
Pencroft then twisted the piece of paper into the shape of a cone, as smokers do in a high wind, and poked it in among the moss.
Hold your breath while Pencroft strikes the match on a stone.
The match catches; the paper catches; the moss catches. Fire. Pencroft roasts the eggs under the cinders, fifty ways known and only one possible.
Neb and Spilett have come back along the shore, and Neb sits down with his face in his hands. Speak to him.
Ah!" cried Neb, "if my master was here, he would know what to do!
Nothing to the north: no trace of the engineer, or of Top.
Herbert has an egg ready for Neb. Go with him.
Neb," said Herbert, running to him, "we will find him! God will give him back to us! But in the meantime you are hungry, and you must eat something.
They eat round the first fire on the island, and sleep in turns to keep it alive.
A grouse's feather
The 26th of March: the inventory
Spilett makes a list of everything the four possess. What is on it?
The clothes they stand in, a notebook, and a watch: nothing else
A box of tools and a gun
That comes later. From somewhere.
They had nothing, save the clothes which they were wearing at the time of the catastrophe.
🔥 Keeping the fire
The fire must never go out again. What does Herbert suggest, if it does?
Burnt linen, which catches a spark like tinder
Waiting for lightning
Burnt linen," replied the boy. "That could in case of need serve for tinder.
Walk up the river into the forest with Pencroft and Herbert, to hunt.
Herbert has seen a bird with bright feathers. Ask him what it is.
That must be a jacamar," said Herbert, trying to get nearer.
How clumsy I am!" cried Herbert.
A couroucou's feather
A flock of couroucous is in the trees: Herbert knocks some down with stones. Pick up five where they fell.
Bright red and green.
Pencroft has a plan for the grouse. Hear it.
Lines of creeper, with hooks of thorn, baited with little red worms, laid by the nests; hide, and pull. Herbert claps his hands when the first grouse is caught.
Hide behind the tree with Pencroft and Herbert, holding the lines, and keep still.
Six grouse and the couroucous on a string. They will eat well. But a storm is coming in from the east.
▶ Back to the Chimneys
The night of the 26th: the storm
Spilett is out on the shore in the rising wind. Go to him.
We are going to have a dirty night, Mr. Spilett!" said the sailor: "Petrels delight in wind and rain.
Spilett asks how far the car was from shore when the engineer fell. Two cables' lengths at most: twelve hundred feet.
The storm breaks. Get back into the Chimneys.
Keep the fire alight through the storm, while the sea booms against the rocks.
Some two hours before morning, Pencroft is shaken awake: Herbert has heard a dog barking outside, in the storm.
Pencroft says it's not possible. What does Herbert do?
Goes out into the storm with a burning branch, calling
Goes back to sleep
Waits until morning
An armful of dry wood was thrown on the embers. The passage was lighted up with a bright flame.
Out into the wind, with a torch. Find the dog.
It is Top: soaked, exhausted, barking. He came alone. Take hold of his collar.
Top turns and runs back the way he came, barking: follow me. The dog has come for them.
Sand from the cave
The 27th of March: the dunes to the north
Follow Top north along the dunes, more than a mile, to a hollow in the sand.
Neb is there, kneeling beside a man lying on a bed of seaweed. Ask him.
Living?" he cried.
Neb does not move. Then Spilett puts his ear to the engineer's chest.
He lives!" said he.
Spilett says they must bring him round. What do they do first?
Rub him hard to bring back the warmth, and give him water
Carry him straight back through the storm
We will save him!" exclaimed the reporter.
Help rub the engineer's arms and chest, to bring the life back into him.
He opens his eyes. Speak to the engineer.
He is weak, but his first thought is a question: island, or continent? And then: how did he get here, a mile from the sea, above high water, on a bed of seaweed?
Neb found his master already lying here, sheltered, out of reach of the waves. Who carried him?
Nobody knows: Top could not have, and Neb found him so
He walked, in his sleep
Harding remembers nothing after the wave.
It is a most extraordinary thing!
Pencroft goes to look for footprints in the sand.
A footprint in the sand
Look for footprints round the hollow in the dunes: find four, and look at them closely.
A footprint. But whose?
Footprints?" exclaimed Pencroft.
The prints fit Harding's own boots. But he does not remember walking. A mystery, the first.
A capybara's bristle
💧 The fire is out
The sea came up into the Chimneys in the storm, and the fire is out: and no second match. Pencroft is in despair.
▶ Tell the captain
Pencroft tells the engineer. Listen.
But, I repeat, that we haven't any fire!" "Pooh!" "Nor any means of relighting it!" "Nonsense!
